title: China's property bust is spilling across its borders
gist: PIIE's Tianlei Huang argues the 'second China shock' in exports is less a subsidy story than a balance-sheet one: China's current account surplus rose from 0.7% of GDP in 2019 to 3.7% in 2025 mainly because the post-2021 housing bust cut household capital formation by 4.1 points of GDP while household saving fell only 0.1 point, and government borrowing (saving-investment balance down 4.8 points) absorbed but did not fully offset the excess. His conclusion is that tariffs treat symptoms, the surplus likely widens further before it narrows, and only bigger consumption-directed fiscal transfers — or equities replacing housing as the household investment vehicle — would genuinely rebalance.

themes.theme: Housing bust as the real engine of China's surplus

insights.claim: China's current account surplus rose from 0.7 percent of GDP in 2019 to 3.7 percent in 2025, with customs data showing an even larger goods surplus than the balance-of-payments figures.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: A five-fold surplus expansion in six years is the quantitative backdrop for every trade-barrier headline; size the tariff/FX risk off 3.7% of GDP, not off anecdote.
insights.quote: China's current account surplus rose from 0.7 percent of GDP in 2019 to 3.7 percent in 2025.
insights.locator: China's rising reliance on exports

insights.claim: The dominant driver of China's widening external surplus is the bursting of the housing bubble since 2021, not industrial subsidies: when households stopped buying homes and developers curtailed construction, domestic investment fell far faster than saving.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: If the surplus is a saving-investment identity problem, it will not respond to subsidy negotiations or tariffs — position for a persistent Chinese goods glut regardless of trade policy outcomes.
insights.quote: Those policies matter, but they are only part of the explanation. A deeper force is the aftermath of the bursting of China's housing bubble since 2021.

insights.claim: Chinese household gross capital formation fell 4.1 percentage points of GDP (from 13.0% to 8.9%) between 2010-20 and 2021-24, while household saving fell only 0.1 point, widening the household saving-investment surplus by 3.9 points to 12.8% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
entities: National Bureau of Statistics of China
insights.so_what: The single largest swing factor in global imbalances right now is Chinese homebuying; track new-home sales as the leading indicator for the surplus and for global goods-price disinflation.

insights.claim: The popular narrative that Chinese consumers turned newly frugal is wrong — household saving rates were broadly stable; what changed is that households stopped channeling saving into housing.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Policies aimed at 'confidence' or coaxing lower saving rates miss the mechanism; the recoverable demand is an investment channel, so watch for an alternative asset outlet rather than a saving-rate collapse.
insights.quote: China's external surplus did not rise because Chinese households suddenly became more frugal. Household saving remained broadly stable.

insights.claim: Because China's flow-of-funds data do not split household capital formation, the author infers residential investment dominates it from pre-2017 data showing rural household fixed asset investment was under 10 percent of total household gross capital formation.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
entities: National Bureau of Statistics of China
insights.so_what: The housing attribution rests on an inference, not a direct series — a modest caveat when leaning on this thesis, and a reminder that Chinese sectoral data require proxies.

themes.theme: Fiscal absorption is the hidden shock absorber

insights.claim: China's general government saving swung down 3.7 percentage points of GDP (from +3.2% to -0.5%) while its public investment rose 1.1 points, pushing the government saving-investment balance 4.8 points deeper into deficit to -7.2% of GDP in 2021-24.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Beijing is already running a far larger effective deficit than headline budget figures imply; fiscal space for the next stimulus round is narrower than consensus assumes.

insights.claim: Government borrowing absorbed most of the extra surplus generated by households and financial institutions, so without the fiscal expansion China's current account surplus would have risen far more dramatically than it did.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Any Chinese fiscal consolidation mechanically exports a bigger surplus abroad — a fiscal-tightening headline in Beijing is a bearish signal for global manufacturers, not a benign one.
insights.quote: Without this fiscal expansion, China's current account surplus would have risen much more dramatically.

insights.claim: The collapse of land-related revenue after the housing bust, alongside pandemic-era fiscal pressures, is directly named as the cause of the plunge in Chinese government saving to negative territory.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Local government fiscal stress and the export surplus are the same story; expect continued LGFV/credit strain as long as land revenue stays impaired.

insights.claim: Despite the sharp fiscal widening, China's national saving-investment balance still rose 0.2 percentage point to average 2.0 percent of GDP in 2021-24, showing the offset was incomplete.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Marginal analysis: the required additional Chinese fiscal impulse to neutralize the external surplus is measurable and has not yet been delivered.

insights.claim: Chinese financial institutions widened their saving-investment surplus by 1.1 percentage points of GDP (to 2.5%), with saving up 0.9 point and capital formation down 0.2 point.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: A less-watched contributor to the surplus — bank sector retained earnings are quietly adding to China's excess saving alongside households.

insights.claim: Part of the larger surplus run by Chinese financial institutions may trace back to Beijing's earlier crackdown on shadow banking, per an Economist analysis cited by the author.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Suggests a regulatory own-goal channel: deleveraging campaigns can raise the external surplus, an unintended consequence worth pricing into future Chinese regulatory tightening.
insights.locator: As The Economist suggested in a September 2023 article

insights.claim: Chinese nonfinancial enterprises' saving-investment balance was essentially unchanged at -6.1 percent of GDP across 2010-20 and 2021-24, with saving and investment both rising about 0.6 point.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Corporate China is not the source of the imbalance — rules out the 'overcapacity investment binge' framing as the marginal driver of the surplus swing.

themes.theme: Housing busts as a repeatable global-imbalance template

insights.claim: Across 11 global housing crises since 1985 — including the US and Japan, excluding China's ongoing one — current account balances rose by an average of 4 percentage points of GDP within five years of the bubble bursting, per Zhao and Guo (2026).
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: A base rate to anchor forecasts: if China follows the template from a 2021 peak, the surplus expansion still has room to run through roughly 2026.
insights.quote: current account balances increased by an average of 4 percentage points of GDP within five years of the bubble bursting
insights.locator: Zhao and Guo (2026) find that across 11 housing crises

insights.claim: The transmission mechanism is generic — investment collapses faster than saving after a housing bust — but China's scale as the world's second-largest economy and dominant manufacturer makes the spillover uniquely large.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Reusable model for any post-bubble economy; here it implies the pain is concentrated in tradable-goods competitors rather than being diffuse.
insights.quote: But because China is the world's second-largest economy and a dominant force in global manufacturing, its domestic imbalances are transmitted abroad on an unusually large scale, inflicting pain on some exporting countries and their industries.
insights.locator: This pattern is not unique to China

insights.claim: Current shares of China's surplus in GDP remain below the extraordinary levels of the 2007-09 global financial crisis era, but the absolute dollar amounts are far larger.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Ratio-based comfort is misleading — the absorbable volume of Chinese goods in world markets is the binding constraint, which argues for more protectionism ahead than GDP-share comparisons suggest.
insights.quote: Although these shares remain below the extraordinary levels seen around the 2007-09 global financial crisis, the absolute amounts are enormous.

insights.claim: The widening gap between China's customs-reported trade surplus and its balance-of-payments figures has sparked economist debate over the accuracy of China's official BOP data, with Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations a leading skeptic.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Official Chinese surplus data may understate reality — the true excess-saving outflow, and therefore the pressure on global asset prices and trade politics, could be larger than 3.7% of GDP.

themes.theme: Outlook, rebalancing paths, and the tariff critique

insights.claim: China's external imbalance will likely get worse before it gets better: as long as households stay reluctant to buy homes, depressed household investment keeps pushing excess saving abroad absent higher consumption, a business investment revival, or a bigger deficit.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Base case is a rising, not peaking, Chinese surplus — bearish for competing exporters' margins, supportive of continued global goods disinflation and further trade-barrier escalation.
insights.quote: China's external imbalance may get worse before it gets better.
insights.locator: The imbalance may worsen before it improves

insights.claim: A plausible but far-from-assured rebalancing path is equities replacing housing as the destination for Chinese household investment, with higher valuations prompting share issuance that funds new corporate investment.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Gives a macro rationale for Beijing tolerating or encouraging an equity bull market; a sustained China equity rally would be an early tell that the surplus is set to narrow.
insights.quote: One possible, though far from assured, path toward rebalancing would be for equities to replace housing as a more important destination for household investment.
insights.locator: One possible, though far from assured

insights.claim: A rising Chinese stock market alone would not guarantee an investment revival if companies remain pessimistic about future demand.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Caution against treating an A-share rally as a rebalancing signal — confirm with capex and equity-issuance data before fading the surplus trade.
insights.quote: But a rising stock market alone would not guarantee an investment revival, particularly if companies remain pessimistic about future demand.
insights.locator: But a rising stock market alone

insights.claim: The most effective policy fix is larger, better-targeted fiscal expansion aimed at household transfers and the social safety net to lift consumption and cut precautionary saving — explicitly more effective than additional support for manufacturing production.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Distinguish stimulus types: supply-side manufacturing support worsens the imbalance, transfer-based stimulus narrows it — the composition of the next Chinese package matters more than its size for global exporters.
insights.quote: Greater public spending, particularly on household transfers and the social safety net, could support domestic consumption and reduce precautionary saving. This action would be more effective in addressing the underlying imbalance than providing additional support to manufacturing production.
insights.locator: A more direct response to these imbalances

insights.claim: Tariffs on Chinese products address only symptoms, since the deeper cause sits inside China — households not investing in housing, weak private domestic demand, and insufficient government offset.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Implies trade barriers will keep multiplying without resolving the flow — the export surge diverts to third markets rather than disappearing; watch transshipment hubs and non-US/EU trade defense actions.
insights.quote: But tariffs directed at Chinese products address only the symptoms of the problem.
insights.locator: China's trading partners are right to pay attention

insights.claim: The combination of surging Chinese exports and sluggish Chinese imports has already prompted many countries across developed and developing economies to impose new trade barriers.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Protectionism is broadening beyond the US and EU into developing-country trade defense — a rising cost line for Chinese exporters and for global supply-chain routing.
